newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia's inter-company debt grows to $1.4 billion.
newsitem.headline: Serbia's inter-company debt grows to $1.4 billion.

text.p: Serbia's inter-company debt grew to 8.5 billion dinars ($1.44 billion) at the end of May and analysts said on Thursday it was a threat to the economy.

"The rising number of insolvent firms is like a stone around the neck of the healthy part of the economy and a threat which could bring many successful firms to their knees and bankruptcy," said one analyst, who asked not to be named.
"Firms who cannot pay their liabilites should simply disappear from the market and allow the rest of the economy to develop," the analyst told Reuters.

The number of permanently insolvent companies in Serbia rose by 128 to 20,331 at the end of May compared to the end of April. Another 11,098 firms had occasional difficulties in meeting their liabilities, the Serbian Chamber of Commerce said in its latest report.
Their matured but unpaid liabilities in May grew by 6.5 percent to 8.58 billion dinars compared to 8.06 billion a month ago.
"What is worrying is that unpaid liabilities at the end of May rose by 62 percent since December last year," said Milosav Filipovic, a member of the Chamber's managing board.
"The problem is also that the total amount of internal debt exceeds the volume of the available funds in the entire economy".
Private firms account for 86.7 percent of the total number of insolvent firms. But socially-owned and mixed enterprises represent the lion's share of unpaid liabilities, or 79.5 percent.
"Social-ownership and the government's intention to cushion lossmaking state companies are among the main reasons for the lack of financial discipline," the analyst said.
"And the fact that managers of the state-controlled firms are at the same time government ministers additionally worsens the situation," the analyst said.
Some 80 percent of the outstanding debts relates to three sectors -- industry and mining (50.3 percent), trade (15 percent) and financial and other services (14 percent).
The metal complex, food-processing, the production and processing of chemical goods, the power industry and coal production are the worst hit.
"Serbia's oil and electric power companies alone account for some five billion dinars of internal debt," said Momir Pavlicevic, vice-president of the republic's Chamber.

A proposal has been made to place 17,352 firms, or 58.6 percent of all insolvent firms, under receivership. They employ 476,054 workers and their unpaid liabilities account for 94 percent of the total internal debt.
Receivership has so far been instituted for only 1,273 companies with 14,789 employees.
"Who is protecting whom? It is obvious that creditors, both banks and firms, are paying the bill while the debtors are protected," Filipovic said.
Analysts saw the obligatory multilateral debt compensation proposed by the central bank simply as an attempt to cure the consequences rather than remove the cause of the disease.

"Internal debt will start to accumulate again. Without genuine privatisation, a strict rule of law and rigid financial discipline, any improvement in debt payments is unlikely," the analyst said. -- Gordana Kukic, Belgrade Newsroom +381 11 311 4254
